title: Technical deep dive: model tuning (Llama/Mistral/Qwen, MoE, RoPE)
summary: Deep technical session between Redwood SEs and HelixAI platform/infra team covering model-specific tuning knobs for Llama/Mistral/Qwen family. Focus areas: profiling latency and throughput, KV cache warm/cold behavior, batching and continuous batching tradeoffs, int8/4 quantization artifacts, MoE routing CPU/GPU costs and gating, and RoPE scaling impacts on long-context performance. Agreed to run a joint benchmark (Helix test prompts + Redwood harness) and share kernel-level traces and a quantization checklist.
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark harness and example load script (by 2026-10-25)
HelixAI to provide 1k real-world prompts and representative long-context sequences (by 2026-10-23)
Schedule follow-up run to test MoE routing delta under 2 batching profiles (by 2026-11-02)
Send security and VPC deployment checklist (Redwood Solutions)
SE to provide quantization experiment notes and config

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-10-21
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Leo Chen (Redwood Infra SWE), Sofia Ruiz (Redwood Solutions), Marta Gomez (HelixAI), Ethan Shaw (HelixAI), Priya Nair (HelixAI)

Auto-generated summary: Technical deep dive on model-specific tuning across Llama/Mistral/Qwen families focusing on runtime, KV cache and MoE routing costs.

---- Transcript ----
[00:00] Redwood-Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, happy friday — we want to dive into the tuning notes we promised after your perf run last week. quick roll call?
[00:08] Customer-Marta: Hi, yeah Marta here, plus Ethan and Priya on our side. thanks for making time.
[00:12] Redwood-Ravi: hi Marta, Ethan, Priya. we'll try to keep high level but get into kernel and batching details.
[00:18] Redwood-Leo: quick note — we pulled the trace you sent into our profiler, some timestamps looked off but we can still reason about kv cache misses.
[00:26] Customer-Ethan: let's start with the long context behaviour — we saw p95 jump after 2k tokens, wondering if that's rope related or just memory thrash.
[00:34] Redwood-Ravi: good q. short answer: often it's RoPE scaling + attention compute shape changes; plus k/v cache eviction patterns on your inference infra.
[00:42] Redwood-Sofia: we also noted batching behavior matters — continuous batching can hide some RoPE overhead but increase latency tail if the coalescing window is too large.
[00:50] Customer-Priya: sorry do you mean coalescing window like the batching timeout? we have it set to 20ms right now.
[00:56] Redwood-Ravi: yes exactly. 20ms is in the midrange; for your 50RPS workload with long sequences, that can push p95 up when you have a few large sequences in queue.
[01:05] Customer-Marta: can you explain how kv cache warm vs cold looks in practice? our logs show a burst in GPU memory use during first 10 tokens of a session.
[01:13] Redwood-Leo: that's classic cold-kv behaviour. first requests write a lot of KV state; with RoPE scaling some libs also allocate extra buffers. after warmup, subsequent tokens are cheaper. we saw similar in Llama family where the initial step is heavier.
[01:24] Customer-Ethan: is that consistent across Mistral and Qwen too? we ran a quick smoke and Mistral seemed smoother but Qwen had spikes.
[01:31] Redwood-Ravi: Mistral's attention implementation often has different kernel shapes — it's more friendly to continuous batching which reduces reshuffle overhead. Qwen sometimes uses fused attention kernels that are great at steady-state but can spike when routing or MoE-style layers kick in.
[01:44] Customer-Priya: MoE — that's big for us. we saw a CPU-side routing overhead in our MoE runs; GPU stayed underutilized because routing decided small expert sets, but CPU was the bottleneck.
[01:53] Redwood-Sofia: yes we see that in hybrid deploys. MoE routing costs are often split: CPU for gating/scoring, GPU for expert execution. if routing isn't batched on the CPU side you get host-side stalls.
[02:03] Customer-Marta: any immediate mitigations? we don't want to rip out MoE but performance hit is concerning.
[02:08] Redwood-Ravi: a couple tactics: (1) route batching — aggregate gating computations across requests to amortize cost, (2) use lightweight gating approximations during peak, (3) control expert fanout to reduce memcopy pressure. We can show config examples.
[02:20] Customer-Ethan: about quantization — we tried int8 and saw hallucination rate increase on certain prompt types. is that expected?
[02:26] Redwood-Leo: yes, int8 can change logits distribution slightly; for instruction-following prompts or tasks sensitive to small token-prob deltas, you may see quality regressions. int4 is even riskier but can work with per-channel calibration and selective per-layer fallback (mixed-precision).
[02:39] Customer-Priya: do you have a recommended checklist for quantization experiments? we want to automate regressions detection.
[02:44] Redwood-Sofia: we'll share a quantization cookbook. short checklist: baseline with fp16, run int8 quant on subset of eval prompt sets, check nll / ranking shifts, run regression evals on instruction sets, consider per-layer FP16 fallback and re-run. also include soft prompts tests.
[02:57] Customer-Marta: ok, good. how do we measure cost delta versus latency tradeoffs? our finance team cares about per-token cost but dev team wants low p95.
[03:05] Redwood-Ava: we typically report three numbers: cost per generated token at steady-state, p50/p95 latency under representative batching, and worst-case cold-start for session priming. we'll share a template — you can plug in dedicated GPU pricing and expected concurrency.
[03:18] Customer-Ethan: about VPC/on-prem — we have a colo with limited NIC bandwidth; we suspect KV cache eviction is thrashing over the network when autoscaling.
[03:26] Redwood-Ravi: network-bound KV caching is an important factor. our private deploys support local KV pinning to avoid remote fetches; for your colo, we'd recommend enabling local shard affinity and increasing prefetch window so the runtime keeps hot kv locally.
[03:39] Customer-Priya: does Redwood's runtime support offline quantized models in the private package? we don't want model artifacts leaving premises.
[03:45] Redwood-Sofia: yes, the private bundle supports on-prem quantized artifacts and KMS integration. we can integrate your HSM for key ops. we'll also provide audit logs for model loads.
[03:56] Customer-Marta: you mentioned kernel selection earlier — how automatic is it? sometimes our codepath ended up using a fallback kernel that was much slower.
[04:03] Redwood-Leo: runtime uses a policy based on sequence length distribution, model arch tags (e.g., Qwen vs Mistral), and measured steady-state perf. but there are heuristics and a cold-start path can pick a fallback until we gather stats. you can pin kernels in the config if you need deterministic behaviour.
[04:20] Customer-Ethan: interesting. can you pin at layer granularity? we had a fused attention that segmented poorly with RoPE scale.
[04:27] Redwood-Ravi: yes layer-level overrides are supported in Dedicated/Private. recommended only for experiments; we also support rollout flags so you can canary kernel changes.
[04:36] Customer-Priya: circling back to RoPE — we saw an odd token decay artefact beyond 8k tokens on Llama v2 variant. is that known?
[04:44] Redwood-Ravi: token decay often stems from RoPE extrapolation and the way positional embeddings wrap. some model families apply scaled RoPE which needs consistent rotary base; if the model uses relative position clipping you can see drift. also some inference libs don't correctly rescale on export which causes degradation at long contexts.
[04:59] Customer-Marta: is there an easy test to isolate RoPE scaling issues?
[05:03] Redwood-Leo: yes — run a sin/cos interpolation probe and compare logits across increasing context lengths on fp16 and quantized runs. if logits drift systematically that's a RoPE mismatch. we'll share a script.
[05:16] Customer-Ethan: about batching — we run a mix of short chatty sessions and occasional long document generation. how should we set batching thresholds and coalescing windows?
[05:24] Redwood-Sofia: recommend two queues: low-latency small-window for chat (e.g., 5ms, small batch cap) and a background path for document generation with larger window (50-100ms) and larger max-batch. you can route by route or by request header indicating expected length.
[05:37] Customer-Priya: does Redwood runtime do prefix caching for multi-turn to avoid re-encoding the entire context? we're seeing repeated encoder cost.
[05:44] Redwood-Ravi: yes we support prefix/KV caching with reference counting and TTLs. typical pattern: cache per-session up to N tokens, maintain a fingerprint so you can quickly validate cache hit. your TTL tuning will affect memory in long-lived chat sessions.
[05:56] Customer-Marta: let's talk numbers — in your tests what p95 difference did you see between fused attention vs standard on Qwen at 1.5k tokens?
[06:03] Redwood-Leo: ballpark: fused kernel at steady-state was ~40% lower p50 and ~25% lower p95 for batches >=8 on Qwen 13B. but at small batches (<=2) the difference collapses and sometimes fused had higher p95 due to compilation overhead.
[06:18] Customer-Ethan: good to know; our typical production batch size is 4.
[06:21] Redwood-Ava: then you might get moderate wins; worth testing.
[06:24] Customer-Priya: you mentioned gating approximations earlier for MoE — can you elaborate on safe approximations that don't blow up quality?
[06:30] Redwood-Ravi: yes: top-k gating with temperature smoothing, or using a lightweight linear gating net on CPU which approximates the heavy gating net. also you can fall back to dense route for some layers during peak. all of these need regression checks.
[06:44] Customer-Marta: action item: we'll want a benchmark that toggles those approximations.
[06:49] Redwood-Ava: noted. we'll provide the harness.
[06:52] Customer-Ethan: about memory — we saw GPU mem 95% during peak; are there runtime knobs to trade mem for a bit more latency?
[06:58] Redwood-Leo: yes, activation recompute and offloading are knobs. you can reduce KV per-token retention (shorter TTL) or use activation checkpointing to trade compute for mem. for latency sensitive paths we avoid recompute, but for batchy background jobs it's fine.
[07:10] Customer-Priya: any guidance on autoscaling policies for Dedicated? we auto-scale on GPU util but that caused thrash.
[07:16] Redwood-Sofia: autoscale on smoothed throughput and queue depth rather than instantaneous GPU util. include a warmup window and scale incrementally. also pre-warm KV on new nodes with a lightweight prefetch.
[07:29] Customer-Marta: you mentioned prefetch — does that add network overhead? our colo NIC is limited.
[07:33] Redwood-Ravi: yes prefetch trades network for lower cold-start latency. tune fanout and parallelism to avoid saturating the NIC. for your environment we might suggest local pinning and smaller prefetch batches.
[07:46] Customer-Ethan: let's talk about observability — we'd like token-level breakdowns and attribution to model layers for p95 spikes. is that possible?
[07:53] Redwood-Leo: we expose token-level timers including time-in-queue, kernel exec, host pre/post, kv fetches; for layer-level attribution we emit sampled traces due to overhead. you can enable sampling rate to 1% to get detailed flamegraphs.
[08:07] Customer-Priya: sampling is fine. how big is the trace artifact? we have limited log retention.
[08:12] Redwood-Sofia: traces are compressed; typical 1% sampling at 10k qps is under 1GB/day but varies. you can store externally to your S3 bucket in private deploy.
[08:26] Customer-Marta: are there known mismatches when exporting models from your training infra to runtime w.r.t RoPE or layernorms?
[08:33] Redwood-Ravi: yes two common things: custom RoPE implementations that rely on training-time scaling and layernorm eps differences. ensure export tool preserves numerical eps and rotary base; we have an export checklist.
[08:47] Customer-Ethan: ok, let's make sure our training exports and the runtime profiles are aligned.
[08:50] Redwood-Ava: i'll share the export checklist and mapping doc.
[08:54] Customer-Priya: one more on quantization — you said per-channel calibration for int4. do you recommend symmetric or asymmetric quant?
[08:59] Redwood-Leo: per-channel symmetric is often simpler and stable, but asymmetric can better capture bias in activations. calibration set matters more than scheme. try both on a small sample.
[09:11] Customer-Marta: circling to next steps and ownership — can someone recap?
[09:15] Redwood-Ava: sure — Ravi will provide kernel-level tracing guide and sample flags; Leo will share fused vs fallback performance numbers we saw for Qwen; Sofia will send quantization cookbook and private deploy checklist with KMS notes; I'll share pricing/budget template and benchmark harness. Marta/Priya/Ethan will provide prompts and run smoke quant tests and upload results.
[09:33] Customer-Marta: thanks. can we schedule the benchmark run next tuesday?
[09:36] Redwood-Ava: we can aim for 2026-11-02 for the coordinated run, I'll send calendar invite.
[09:41] Customer-Ethan: noted. any blockers on us getting the harness?
[09:44] Redwood-Ravi: none; we'll share via S3 link and a small README.
[09:48] Customer-Priya: thanks, helpful session.
[09:50] Redwood-Ava: great, thanks all. we'll follow up with notes and artifacts.

End of call.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker mislabels and timestamp jitter from audio transcription. References to kernels/fused attention/KV cache are paraphrased from SE comments. Links shared: Redwood benchmark harness (s3://redwood-harness/helix/2026-10-21), quantization cookbook (link in follow-up email).
